term:Safe.deep_dive: The NIST trustworthiness characteristic: the system does not, under defined conditions, endanger human life, health, property, or environment — engineered through safe design, testing against failure modes, and the ability to halt. Safety is the characteristic where AI governance meets classic product safety.
term:Safe.exam_tip: One of NIST's seven — and safety-critical scenarios (health, vehicles, infrastructure) elevate it to the controlling consideration.

term:Safety & Security Chapter (GPAI CoP.deep_dive: The GPAI Code of Practice chapter binding only systemic-risk model providers: a safety and security framework, state-of-the-art model evaluations, systemic risk identification/analysis/mitigation, serious-incident reporting, and cybersecurity protections for model weights and infrastructure — operationalizing AI Act Article 55.
term:Safety & Security Chapter (GPAI CoP.exam_tip: Only systemic-risk GPAI providers — the Transparency and Copyright chapters bind everyone; this one doesn't.

term:Sample.deep_dive: A subset drawn from a population for training or evaluation — the statistical unit whose selection determines representativeness. Sampling method (random, stratified, convenience) is a governance-relevant choice: biased frames yield biased models regardless of downstream care.
term:Sample.exam_tip: Interrogate the sampling frame when a model fails a subgroup — the flaw usually predates training.

term:Secondary Use.deep_dive: Processing data for a purpose other than the one it was collected for — AI training being the canonical modern example. GDPR requires a compatibility analysis (link between purposes, context, data nature, consequences, safeguards) or a fresh lawful basis plus transparency — silent repurposing is the violation.
term:Secondary Use.exam_tip: Data on hand ≠ data available for training — the compatibility-or-new-basis analysis is the required step.

term:Secure and Resilient.deep_dive: The NIST trustworthiness characteristic pairing protection with recovery: withstand unauthorized access and adversarial attack (secure), and maintain function or degrade gracefully through disruption (resilient) — covering the ML-specific attack surface from poisoning to model theft.
term:Secure and Resilient.exam_tip: NIST bundles the pair as one characteristic of the seven — security keeps attackers out, resilience survives what gets through.

term:Security.deep_dive: Protecting AI assets — data, models, pipelines, endpoints — against the classic triad threats plus ML-native attacks: data poisoning, model inversion, membership inference, adversarial examples, prompt injection, model theft. The AI Act makes cybersecurity an explicit high-risk requirement; MITRE ATLAS catalogs the threat landscape.
term:Security.exam_tip: AI security = traditional security + the ML attack family — answers covering only conventional controls are incomplete.

term:Security Testing.deep_dive: Probing AI systems for exploitable weaknesses — conventional (access, injection, infrastructure) plus ML-specific: can training data be poisoned, can the model be inverted or stolen, do adversarial inputs flip outputs, do prompts jailbreak it. Red teaming is its adversarial, exercise-style form.
term:Security Testing.exam_tip: Match attack to test: poisoning (training-time), inversion/membership (privacy), adversarial examples (inference-time), injection (LLM) — coverage questions expect the full family.

term:Self-Aware AI.deep_dive: The functionality ladder's theoretical summit: systems with consciousness and knowledge of their own states — pure hypothesis, no engineering path, useful in the taxonomy as the boundary marker between real capability tiers and science fiction.
term:Self-Aware AI.exam_tip: Theoretical, like theory-of-mind AI above limited-memory — ladder-placement questions expect 'does not exist.'

term:Semi-Supervised Learning.deep_dive: Training on a small labeled set plus a large unlabeled one — the labeled data anchors the task, the unlabeled mass refines the representation. The economics: labels are expensive, raw data is cheap, and semi-supervision buys accuracy without the labeling bill.
term:Semi-Supervised Learning.exam_tip: Small labeled + large unlabeled = semi-supervised — positioned between supervised and unsupervised in the paradigm taxonomy.

term:Semi-Supervised Machine Learning.deep_dive: The same paradigm under its ISO 22989 name: machine learning using both labeled and unlabeled data during training — worth having as a distinct vocabulary entry because standards documents use the full formal term.
term:Semi-Supervised Machine Learning.exam_tip: Identical concept to semi-supervised learning — recognize both phrasings as one paradigm.

term:Sensitive Data.deep_dive: The umbrella for data whose misuse causes elevated harm — GDPR special categories, financial data, children's data, precise location — demanding heightened protection wherever it flows. AI's twist: models infer sensitive data from innocuous inputs, creating sensitive processing without sensitive collection.
term:Sensitive Data.exam_tip: Inference creates sensitive data too — a model deriving health status from shopping behavior is processing sensitive data.

term:Sentiment Analysis.deep_dive: The NLP task of classifying emotional tone — positive/negative/neutral, or finer emotional states — powering brand monitoring, feedback triage, and market analysis. Governance shadow: sentiment inference about individuals edges toward emotion recognition, which the AI Act prohibits in workplaces and schools.
term:Sentiment Analysis.exam_tip: Aggregate sentiment on reviews is minimal-risk; emotion inference about individuals at work or school crosses into prohibited territory.

term:Soft Computing.deep_dive: The tolerance-for-imprecision family: fuzzy logic, neural networks, evolutionary computation — approaches that trade exactness for tractability on messy real-world problems, contrasted with hard computing's precise algorithms. Mostly historical/taxonomic vocabulary today.
term:Soft Computing.exam_tip: Recognize as the umbrella for approximate methods (fuzzy, neural, evolutionary) — terminology awareness suffices.

term:Special Category Data.deep_dive: GDPR Article 9's protected list: racial/ethnic origin, political opinions, religious/philosophical beliefs, trade-union membership, genetic data, biometric data for identification, health, sex life/orientation — processing prohibited absent a 9(2) condition, DPIA-triggering at scale, and inferable by AI from ordinary data.
term:Special Category Data.exam_tip: Article 6 basis AND Article 9 condition both required — and criminal-offense data (Art 10) is its own separate regime, a nuance distractor.

term:Speech Recognition (STT).deep_dive: Speech-to-text: converting spoken audio into written language — the input side of voice interfaces. Governance angles: voice is biometric-adjacent (speaker identification is biometric processing), accuracy disparities across accents are a fairness pattern, and always-listening devices raise collection questions.
term:Speech Recognition (STT).exam_tip: STT = speech in, text out; TTS is the reverse — and accent-based accuracy gaps are the fairness hook.

term:Speech Synthesis (TTS).deep_dive: Text-to-speech: generating spoken audio from text — now realistic enough that voice cloning enables fraud and deepfake audio, pulling TTS into synthetic-media governance: disclosure duties, consent for voice likeness, and provenance marking.
term:Speech Synthesis (TTS).exam_tip: TTS = text in, speech out — with voice-cloning abuse as the attached risk to name.

term:Speed and Scale.deep_dive: The multiplier characteristic: AI executes decisions in milliseconds across millions of cases, so a single flaw propagates to population scale before humans notice — compressing the window between deployment error and mass harm. It's the quantitative argument for pre-deployment testing and automated monitoring.
term:Speed and Scale.exam_tip: Speed and scale explain why AI governance frontloads: by the time a human sees the problem, it has already happened a million times.

term:Stakeholder (Interested Party).deep_dive: ISO's formal term: any person or organization that can affect, be affected by, or perceive itself affected by a decision or activity — for AI, spanning boards to data subjects to regulators to civil society. Stakeholder determination is an explicit ISO 42001 clause-4 requirement shaping AIMS scope.
term:Stakeholder (Interested Party).exam_tip: 'Interested party' in ISO text = stakeholder — same concept, standards register.

term:Stakeholder Mapping.deep_dive: The structured exercise of identifying stakeholders and charting their interest, influence, and exposure — feeding impact assessments (who could be harmed), governance design (who needs a seat), and communications (who needs to know what). Its omission is why systems surprise the people they affect.
term:Stakeholder Mapping.exam_tip: During risk identification, stakeholder mapping reveals how different groups are differentially affected — its tested purpose.

term:Stress Testing (AI).deep_dive: Pushing the system past comfortable conditions before launch: peak loads, degraded infrastructure, malformed inputs, adversarial prompts, edge-case scenarios — measuring latency, resource ceilings, failover behavior, and failure gracefulness. The readiness gate's empirical core.
term:Stress Testing (AI).exam_tip: Stress testing = operational limits and failure behavior — complementary to accuracy validation, not a substitute.

term:STRIDE.deep_dive: Microsoft's threat-modeling mnemonic — Spoofing, Tampering, Repudiation, Information disclosure, Denial of service, Elevation of privilege — applied to AI pipelines: tampering maps to data poisoning, information disclosure to model inversion, DoS to resource-exhaustion attacks on inference.
term:STRIDE.exam_tip: STRIDE = threat modeling framework (security analysis structure), not an AI-specific control — recognize and map its categories.

term:Sub-Tier Dependencies.deep_dive: The suppliers behind your suppliers: the labeling firms, base-model providers, open-source components, and data brokers your AI vendor relies on — invisible in the contract, present in the risk. TPRM's hardest question is how many tiers down to probe; the answer scales with system criticality.
term:Sub-Tier Dependencies.exam_tip: Vendor risk includes the vendor's vendors — flow-down contract clauses and provenance demands are the tested controls.

term:Subsymbolic AI.deep_dive: The paradigm where knowledge lives in numbers, not symbols: distributed weights, learned representations, no human-readable rules — neural networks being the flagship. Capability high, inspectability low; the opacity that drives explainability requirements is subsymbolic by nature.
term:Subsymbolic AI.exam_tip: Subsymbolic = connectionist = neural (learned, opaque) vs. symbolic (rules, transparent) — one distinction, several labels.

term:Supervised Learning.deep_dive: The labeled-data paradigm: models learn input→output mappings from example pairs — spam/not-spam, price given features — and generalize to new inputs. Most deployed business ML is supervised, which means most deployed ML inherits its labels' quality and bias.
term:Supervised Learning.exam_tip: Labeled input-output pairs = supervised — and the labels are where historical bias enters.

term:Supervised Machine Learning.deep_dive: The ISO 22989 formal name for the same paradigm — machine learning where training data carries target labels the model learns to predict. Dual-listed because standards and exam text use the full term.
term:Supervised Machine Learning.exam_tip: Same concept as supervised learning — one paradigm, two phrasings.

term:Support Vector Machine (SVM).deep_dive: The classic maximum-margin classifier: find the boundary separating classes with the widest buffer, using kernels to handle non-linear structure — a pre-deep-learning workhorse that remains competitive on smaller, structured datasets and more interpretable than neural alternatives.
term:Support Vector Machine (SVM).exam_tip: Recognition-level: classical ML technique, margin-based classification — a 'traditional ML' answer option.

term:Symbolic AI.deep_dive: The rules-and-logic paradigm: knowledge encoded explicitly (ontologies, rules, logic), reasoning by symbol manipulation — expert systems as its production form. Transparent and brittle where learned systems are capable and opaque; the pendulum between the paradigms is AI history in one sentence.
term:Symbolic AI.exam_tip: Symbolic = explicit rules, explainable, brittle; its opposite pole is subsymbolic/connectionist learning.

term:System Card.deep_dive: Documentation for the deployed whole: the assembled system's components, data flows, model interactions, oversight points, and operational context — one level up from model cards, because users experience systems, not models, and risk lives in the assembly.
term:System Card.exam_tip: Model card documents the model; system card documents the assembled deployment — pick the right artifact for the scope.

term:Task.deep_dive: ISO 22989's unit of AI work: the defined function a system performs — classify, translate, rank, generate. Task definition disciplines everything: narrow AI is task-scoped, evaluation is task-relative, and scope creep is task expansion without re-assessment.
term:Task.exam_tip: Terminology anchor — capabilities are defined per task, and approvals attach to tasks, not to models in the abstract.

term:Technical Documentation.deep_dive: The AI Act's evidence dossier (Annex IV): system description, development process, data requirements, risk management, testing, performance, oversight design — prepared before market placement, kept current, retained ten years, and producible on regulatory demand. Conformity's paper trail.
term:Technical Documentation.exam_tip: Annex IV + 10-year retention + must exist before CE marking — the three facts that get tested.

term:Test Data (Evaluation Data).deep_dive: The held-out final exam: data untouched during training and tuning, used once to estimate real-world performance honestly. Its integrity is sacred — leakage from training, or repeated tuning against it, silently converts 'evaluation' into fiction.
term:Test Data (Evaluation Data).exam_tip: Train fits, validation tunes, test evaluates — and tuning on test data is the invalidation pattern to spot.

term:Theory of Mind AI.deep_dive: The hypothetical tier that models other minds: understanding beliefs, intentions, and emotions to interact socially — a functionality-ladder rung above limited memory, below self-awareness, with no deployed instance despite chatbot simulations of empathy.
term:Theory of Mind AI.exam_tip: Theoretical tier — simulated empathy in current chatbots does not qualify; ladder placement is the question.

term:Third-Party Processor.deep_dive: GDPR's outsourced hands: an external entity processing personal data on the controller's documented instructions — cloud platforms, analytics vendors, AI-API providers — bound by Article 28 contracts covering security, sub-processors, audit rights, and breach notice. The controller's accountability never transfers with the data.
term:Third-Party Processor.exam_tip: AI vendors processing your users' data on your instructions are processors — Article 28 DPA required, accountability retained.

term:Third-Party Risk Management (TPRM).deep_dive: The lifecycle discipline for vendor exposure: due diligence before contracting, contractual risk allocation, continuous monitoring during, and orderly exit after — extended for AI to cover training-data provenance, model changes, sub-tier suppliers, and fairness evidence that classic TPRM never asked about.
term:Third-Party Risk Management (TPRM).exam_tip: AI TPRM = classic TPRM + AI-specific probes (provenance, bias evidence, model-change notice) — the extension is what's tested.

term:Trade Secret.deep_dive: IP protection through secrecy: information deriving value from not being known, guarded by reasonable measures — the default protection for model weights, training recipes, and prompt libraries. Fragile by design: disclosure destroys it, so employee prompts pasted into public AI tools are an IP event, not just a privacy one.
term:Trade Secret.exam_tip: Protection requires actual secrecy measures — and feeding confidential data into external AI tools can forfeit trade-secret status.

term:Trained Model.deep_dive: ISO 22989's term for training's product: the parameter-laden artifact ready for inference — versioned, evaluated, documented, and deployed as a unit. Distinguishing 'model' (architecture/concept) from 'trained model' (specific learned instance) keeps versioning and validation talk precise.
term:Trained Model.exam_tip: Each training run yields a distinct trained model — validation and approval attach to the instance, not the architecture.

term:Training (Model Training).deep_dive: The learning process itself: an algorithm iteratively adjusting parameters against data until the model captures the target patterns — compute-intensive, data-hungry, and consequential: everything the data contains, the model absorbs. Training is where governance's data controls pay off or fail.
term:Training (Model Training).exam_tip: Training = patterns from data via iterative learning — and its inputs (data rights, quality, representativeness) are the governed surface.

term:Training and Awareness Program.deep_dive: The organizational competence layer: role-tailored AI education — executive risk literacy, developer governance-by-design, user appropriate-reliance — refreshed as law and technology move, now underwritten by the AI Act's AI-literacy expectations. Culture is a control, and this is how it's built.
term:Training and Awareness Program.exam_tip: Role-tailored beats one-size-fits-all in every training scenario — and AI literacy became a legal expectation in February 2025.

term:Training and Testing.deep_dive: The paired disciplines of the model lifecycle: learn from training data, then verify against data the model never saw — with the discipline being separation. The phrase names the workflow whose corruption (leakage, test-set tuning) invalidates every quality claim downstream.
term:Training and Testing.exam_tip: The separation is the point — any scenario blending training and evaluation data is describing invalidated results.

term:Training Data.deep_dive: The dataset a model learns from — and therefore the single most consequential governance surface in AI: its rights determine legality, its quality determines accuracy, its representativeness determines fairness, its sensitivity determines privacy exposure, and its documentation determines auditability.
term:Training Data.exam_tip: Most model problems trace to training data — rights, quality, representativeness — before they trace to algorithms.

term:Transfer Learning.deep_dive: Reusing learned representations: start from a model trained on one task, adapt it to another — the economics behind the foundation-model era (pretrain once, fine-tune everywhere). Governance inheritance rides along: the base model's biases, data provenance, and license terms transfer with the weights.
term:Transfer Learning.exam_tip: Transfer learning inherits the base model's risks and restrictions — provenance questions don't reset at fine-tuning.

term:Transparency (Organization).deep_dive: ISO 22989 distinguishes the organizational property: openness about activities and decisions — what AI the organization uses, for what, governed how — expressed through notices, reports, and registries, as distinct from any single system's inspectability.
term:Transparency (Organization).exam_tip: Organization-level transparency (we disclose our AI use) vs. system-level (this system's workings are inspectable) — ISO splits them deliberately.

term:Transparency (System).deep_dive: The system-level property: information about a specific system's capabilities, limitations, data, and logic is available to those who need it — the substrate for informed use, effective oversight, and contestable decisions. Companion to explainability: transparency supplies information, explainability makes outputs comprehensible.
term:Transparency (System).exam_tip: Transparency = information availability; explainability = output comprehensibility — the exam's favorite near-synonym split.

term:Transparency Chapter (GPAI CoP).deep_dive: The GPAI Code of Practice chapter binding all signatory providers: model documentation aligned to Annex XI, information packages enabling downstream providers to meet their own obligations (Annex XII), and contact/update practices — operationalizing AI Act Articles 53(1)(a)-(b).
term:Transparency Chapter (GPAI CoP).exam_tip: All GPAI providers — transparency and copyright chapters are universal; only safety & security is systemic-risk-only.

term:Trustworthiness.deep_dive: The summary property: an AI system worthy of justified confidence — NIST decomposes it into seven characteristics (valid & reliable, safe, secure & resilient, accountable & transparent, explainable & interpretable, privacy-enhanced, fair), ISO into properties like robustness, reliability, controllability. Trustworthy AI is the goal-state all frameworks describe from different angles.
term:Trustworthiness.exam_tip: 'Trustworthy AI' is NIST's umbrella — when a question lists characteristics, count them against the seven.

term:Underfitting.deep_dive: The model that never learned: too simple, too constrained, or too starved to capture real patterns — performing poorly on training data and new data alike. Remedies run opposite to overfitting's: more capacity, richer features, longer training.
term:Underfitting.exam_tip: Bad everywhere = underfitting; great on training only = overfitting — the diagnostic pair in one line.

term:Unfair and Deceptive Acts and Pract.deep_dive: The consumer-protection workhorse: FTC Act §5 federally and state mini-FTC acts locally, prohibiting deception (misleading material claims) and unfairness (substantial, unavoidable, unjustified injury) — the enforcement basis for AI-washing, undisclosed bots, and harmful algorithmic practices.
term:Unfair and Deceptive Acts and Pract.exam_tip: UDAP is technology-neutral — AI claims and AI conduct are tested under the same deception/unfairness standards as everything else.

term:Unintended Use.deep_dive: Systems used beyond their intended purpose — a triage assistant becomes the de facto diagnostician, a fraud score leaks into hiring. Foreseeable misuse must be anticipated (warned against, designed against), and material repurposing re-triggers assessment: intended use defines the risk analysis, so new use voids it.
term:Unintended Use.exam_tip: Intended purpose anchors everything (risk class, testing, instructions) — foreseeable misuse is the provider's problem too, not just the user's.

term:Unit Testing.deep_dive: Testing components in isolation — a preprocessing function, a feature transform, a scoring module — before integration compounds failures. In ML pipelines it covers the deterministic scaffolding around the model; the model itself needs statistical evaluation beyond pass/fail assertions.
term:Unit Testing.exam_tip: Unit tests verify pipeline components; model quality needs validation testing — the ladder starts here but can't end here.

term:Unsupervised Learning.deep_dive: Learning without labels: finding structure in raw data — clustering customers, reducing dimensions, flagging anomalies. Its governance edge: discovered patterns can encode sensitive groupings nobody asked for, and anomaly definitions quietly become policy.
term:Unsupervised Learning.exam_tip: No labels, finds structure — clustering and anomaly detection are the recognition examples.

term:Unsupervised Machine Learning.deep_dive: The ISO 22989 formal phrasing of the unlabeled paradigm — machine learning drawing patterns from data without target labels. Dual-listed with its short form because standards text uses the full term.
term:Unsupervised Machine Learning.exam_tip: Same paradigm as unsupervised learning — recognize both names.

term:Use Case.deep_dive: The defined application: what the system does, for whom, in what context, with what success criteria — the unit governance attaches to. Risk classification, impact assessment, and approval all bind to the use case, which is why undocumented new uses are governance violations, not features.
term:Use Case.exam_tip: Approvals attach to use cases, not models — same model, new use case, new assessment.

term:Use Case Assessment.deep_dive: The screening gate for proposed AI applications: value, feasibility, data availability, risk profile, and regulatory exposure evaluated before commitment — where bad ideas die cheap and good ideas acquire their governance requirements. The first formal artifact in a well-run lifecycle.
term:Use Case Assessment.exam_tip: Sequencing: assess the use case before collecting data or building — the earliest and cheapest control gate.

term:User Training.deep_dive: Preparing the humans who operate AI: what the system can and cannot do, how to read its outputs and uncertainty, when to override, how to report anomalies — the counterweight to automation bias and the enabler of meaningful oversight. Deployment readiness includes it; incident postmortems miss it at their peril.
term:User Training.exam_tip: Over-reliance scenarios resolve through user training plus interface design — not through model accuracy improvements alone.

term:Valid and Reliable.deep_dive: NIST's first-listed trustworthiness characteristic — and the framework calls it a precondition: the system measurably does what it claims (valid) and keeps doing it under expected conditions (reliable). Without validity, the other six characteristics are decorations on a system that doesn't work.
term:Valid and Reliable.exam_tip: The foundational NIST characteristic — validity is a necessary condition for trustworthiness; the other six assume it.

term:Validation.deep_dive: Are we building the right thing, and does it meet requirements? — evaluating the trained model against its specified functional, performance, and fairness requirements on data it hasn't seen, before deployment authorizes it. Paired with verification (built right?) in the V&V discipline.
term:Validation.exam_tip: Validation = meets requirements/fit for intended use; verification = built to spec — the V&V split is precise and tested.

term:Validation Data (Development Data).deep_dive: The middle dataset: used during development to tune hyperparameters and compare candidate models — spent data, because decisions were made against it, which is why the untouched test set must render the final verdict.
term:Validation Data (Development Data).exam_tip: Three-way split roles: training fits, validation tunes, test judges — validation data can't double as the final exam.

term:Vendor Agreement.deep_dive: The contract that allocates AI risk between customer and supplier: data-use limits, performance and bias warranties, audit rights, model-change and incident notification, IP and confidentiality terms, liability, and exit portability. For AI vendors it's where governance requirements become enforceable obligations.
term:Vendor Agreement.exam_tip: The AI-specific clauses (data use, bias warranties, change notice, audit rights) are what distinguish an adequate AI vendor agreement from a generic one.

term:Verification.deep_dive: Did we build it right? — confirming the system conforms to its design specifications: code does what the design says, pipeline transforms match documentation, implementation matches architecture. The engineering half of V&V, logically prior to validation's fitness question.
term:Verification.exam_tip: Verification = conformance to spec; validation = fitness for intended purpose — keep the order and the questions straight.

term:Verification & Validation.deep_dive: The paired assurance discipline — verification (built to specification) plus validation (meets requirements and intended use) — institutionalized as a formal lifecycle stage in ISO 22989 and as TEVV (test, evaluation, verification, validation) throughout NIST's framework vocabulary.
term:Verification & Validation.exam_tip: V&V is an ISO lifecycle stage and the VV in NIST's TEVV — both acronyms decompose to the same two questions.

term:Workforce Readiness.deep_dive: Whether the organization's people are prepared for AI — skills to build and govern it, literacy to use it appropriately, and change management for the roles it transforms. A readiness gap is a deployment risk in its own right: capable systems operated by unprepared workforces produce incidents.
term:Workforce Readiness.exam_tip: Readiness assessments include the humans — technology-ready but workforce-unready is a failing state the exam recognizes.

term:Zero-Shot Learning (ZSL).deep_dive: Performing tasks with no task-specific training examples — modern LLMs following novel instructions from pretraining alone. Impressive and treacherous: zero-shot competence is unvalidated competence, with no task-specific evaluation behind it until someone builds one.
term:Zero-Shot Learning (ZSL).exam_tip: Zero-shot = no task examples needed — and its governance corollary: capability without task-specific validation still needs testing before consequential use.
